[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Tensors, Creation, and Memory Layout in PyTorch"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Tensors are the fundamental data structures in PyTorch, enabling high-performance deep learning computations on CPUs and GPUs. Understanding how tensors are created and how their memory is laid out is crucial for writing efficient, optimized code."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Tensors"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"At its core, a tensor is a multi-dimensional array similar to NumPy's ndarray, with the added capability of running on accelerators like GPUs. Tensors maintain metadata about their data type, device placement, and memory layout."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Tensor Creation Methods"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"PyTorch provides numerous ways to instantiate tensors depending on whether you are initializing with raw data, predefined shapes, or random distributions."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"import torch

# Creating a tensor from existing data
data = [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]
x_data = torch.tensor(data)

# Creating tensors with specific shapes and zeros or ones
x_ones = torch.ones(2, 3)
x_zeros = torch.zeros(2, 2)

# Creating tensors with random values
x_rand = torch.rand(3, 3)
print(x_rand)"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Memory Layout: Strides and Storage"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Behind every PyTorch tensor lies a contiguous block of memory called Storage (torch.UntypedStorage). A tensor is simply a view into this storage, defined by a shape, a data type, and strides."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Shape: Defines the size of the tensor along each dimension."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Strides: The number of elements to skip in memory when moving to the next position along a specific axis."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"t = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print("Shape:", t.shape)
print("Strides:", t.stride())"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Contiguous vs Non-Contiguous Tensors"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Operations like transpose or slicing do not copy data; instead, they alter the tensor strides. This creates non-contiguous tensors. Certain hardware operations require data to be contiguous in memory."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"t_transposed = t.t()
print("Is contiguous?", t_transposed.is_contiguous())

# Force memory to be contiguous
t_contiguous = t_transposed.contiguous()
print("Is contiguous now?", t_contiguous.is_contiguous())"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mastering tensor creation and understanding stride-based memory layouts helps prevent silent performance bottlenecks, especially when writing custom layers or interfacing with low-level C++ extensions."}]
